(CNN) -- As the first president-elect with a Facebook page and a YouTube channel, Barack Obama is poised to use the Internet to communicate directly with Americans in a way unknown to previous presidents. Since the election, President-elect Barack Obama has posted weekly video addresses on YouTube. Judging by Obama's savvy use of social-networking sites during his campaign and the interactive nature of his transition team's Web site, Americans can expect a president who bypasses the traditional media's filters while reaching out to citizens for input, observers say. "The rebooting of our democracy has begun," said Andrew Rasiej, founder of Personal Democracy Forum and the techPresident blog. "[Obama] has the potential to transform the relationship between the American public and their democracy." During the presidential race, Obama's campaign won praise for its innovative use of social-networking sites, including Facebook, MySpace and MyBarackObama.com, to announce events, rally volunteers and raise money. Facebook has more than 150 million active users, and the average user has 100 friends on the site, according to the company. iReport.com: Your chance to ask President-elect Obama a question . Obama has more than 1 million MySpace "friends" and more than 3.7 million "supporters" on his official Facebook page -- some 700,000 more than when he was elected in November. His campaign also has a database of almost 13 million supporters and their e-mail addresses. Transition officials hope to transform Obama's vast Web operation and electronic list of supporters into a 21st-century tool to help accomplish his goals as president. They even have a name for this ambitious effort: Obama 2.0. "Obama has invented an alternative media model," said CNN senior political analyst Bill Schneider. "In the old model, the president talks to the people on television [and] the people talk back in polls. In the new model, communication is online, and two-way." Facebook, MySpace, YouTube and Twitter didn't exist when George W. Bush took office eight years ago. But since last November's election, Obama has wasted no time embracing these online communication portals. In recent weeks he has taped weekly video addresses and posted them to YouTube, where most have been viewed hundreds of thousands of times. Obama's staffers also have stopped posting information to social-networking sites since the election, preferring to reach out to constituents through YouTube and Change.gov, the official site of the president-elect's transition team. Visitors to Change.gov can read a frequently updated blog, post their ideas on issues facing the country, and rate others' ideas. Top-rated ideas will be gathered into a briefing book and given to Obama after he takes office. "They want information going not just from them to the voters, but from the voters back to them," Democratic strategist Steve McMahon said Wednesday on CNN's "The Situation Room." "Thirteen million people pushing a button, sending an e-mail to their elected representatives, making a phone call, taking action, is a powerful, powerful lobbying tool." "It's a very smart use of the Internet, to get people to offer ideas," said David All, a Republican Internet strategist. All hopes that Obama and his staff take a similar approach to WhiteHouse.gov, the president's official Web site. The current WhiteHouse.gov site, operated by the Bush administration, contains few interactive features. A statement on the president-elect's transition site says that Obama hopes to "use cutting-edge technologies to create a new level of transparency, accountability, and participation for America's citizens." It's fitting, then, that Obama's inauguration next week could be one of the most watched video events in Internet history. Rasiej expects that hordes of users will be watching online when Obama takes the oath of office, visiting WhiteHouse.gov and refreshing their browsers to capture the moment the site switches to proclaim Obama, not George W. Bush, as president. As president, Obama will likely not just rely on WhiteHouse.gov but use multiple Internet sites and technological tools to build grass-roots support for his agenda, observers say. "[Obama] is using the tools that are available to him today," All told CNN. "The next president will be using some of the same tools, and also some tools that haven't been invented yet."

The 2008 United States presidential election marked a fundamental turning point in modern political history, largely driven by a paradigm shift in how politicians connect with the electorate. When Franklin D. Roosevelt harnessed the power of radio for his "fireside chats" in the 1930s, and John F. Kennedy mastered the visual medium of television in the 1960s, both leaders fundamentally altered the relationship between the American presidency and the electorate. Following the 2008 presidential election, President-elect Barack Obama initiated the next major evolutionary leap in political communication. Facing a rapidly evolving media ecosystem, the incoming administration recognized that the traditional playbook—relying exclusively on press briefings, cable news cycles, and print journalism—was no longer sufficient to build trust and momentum. 

To bypass traditional media filters and connect directly with the public, President-elect Barack Obama utilized social networking platforms, weekly YouTube addresses, and an interactive transition website. For decades, traditional media outlets acted as gatekeepers, deciding which statements were highlighted, contextually framed, or edited down into brief soundbites. By launching platforms like Change.gov—the official transition website—and establishing a presence on emerging social networks like Facebook and Twitter, the Obama team effectively subverted these intermediaries. **Title:** From Cable to Clicks: How CNN, Facebook, and YouTube Reshaped the Information Age

The way humanity consumes news and entertainment has undergone a radical transformation over the past few decades. The era of waiting for the evening paper or tuning in to a single nightly broadcast has given way to an instantaneous, 24/7 stream of information. At the heart of this media revolution are three distinct giants—**CNN**, **Facebook**, and **YouTube**—each representing a different phase in the evolution of modern communication.

When **CNN** (Cable News Network) launched in 1980, it shattered the traditional broadcast model by introducing the world to the 24-hour news cycle. For the first time, viewers could witness history unfolding in real-time, from the Fall of the Berlin Wall to the Persian Gulf War. CNN established the benchmark for breaking news, building a global infrastructure of journalists and bureaus dedicated to constant coverage. However, as the internet matured, even a pioneering cable network faced a new challenge: the rise of user-driven digital platforms.

Enter **Facebook**. Founded as a social networking site for college students, Facebook quickly evolved into a primary news distributor for billions of people worldwide. It changed the dynamic of information consumption from passive viewing to active engagement. Rather than going directly to a news website, users began encountering headlines within their personalized news feeds, curated by algorithms based on likes, shares, and comments. Facebook transformed news into a social experience, allowing users to discuss global events with friends and family, while simultaneously giving news organizations like CNN a powerful new channel to amplify their content. 

Parallel to the social media boom, **YouTube** revolutionized video consumption by democratizing content creation. Launched in 2005, YouTube provided a platform where anyone with a camera could become a broadcaster. It rapidly grew from a repository of viral home videos into a global powerhouse for entertainment, education, and commentary. For legacy media, YouTube became an essential landscape; networks like CNN began publishing live streams, key interview clips, and investigative segments on the platform to reach younger, cord-cutting audiences. Simultaneously, independent creators on YouTube began offering alternative commentary, challenging traditional media outlets for viewers' attention.

Today, these three entities exist in a complex, symbiotic ecosystem. CNN provides the journalistic infrastructure and brand authority; Facebook offers the algorithmic network that makes stories go viral; and YouTube serves as the vast visual library where viewers can stream coverage on demand. 

Together, CNN, Facebook, and YouTube illustrate how media has evolved from a top-down broadcast model into a dynamic, interactive web. While this shift has made information more accessible than ever before, it has also raised critical questions about misinformation, algorithmic bias, and the future of journalism. As technology continues to advance, the interplay between legacy news outlets and digital platforms will remain a central force in shaping public discourse.

**STORY HIGHLIGHTS**
* President-elect Obama plans to adapt his record-breaking digital campaign apparatus for governing.

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — When Franklin D. Roosevelt took to the airwaves for his "fireside chats" in the 1930s, he revolutionized how a president speaks to the American people. John F. Kennedy later mastered the medium of live television. 

Now, as Barack Obama prepares to take the oath of office on January 20, his incoming administration is preparing the next great leap in presidential communication: the era of "Obama 2.0."

Having used social media, target-rich email blasts, and online video to power a historic campaign and raise hundreds of millions of dollars, the President-elect is making it clear that his digital engine will not be turned off once he enters the Oval Office. Instead, his team is attempting to rewire 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue for the Web 2.0 age.

"We are looking at a fundamental shift in how the presidency interacts with the public," said Sarah Bindman, a digital media analyst at the Center for New Media Studies. "The Obama team didn't just use the internet to get elected; they intend to use it as an instrument of governance, pressure, and transparency."

### The Digital Transition: Change.gov

The blueprint for this digital presidency is already visible on Change.gov, the official website of the Obama-Biden transition team. 

Unlike past transitions, which relied heavily on formal press releases and leaks to major news outlets, the Obama team has turned to the web to speak directly to citizens. The site features an "Open Government" portal, encouraging Americans to submit policy ideas, vote on the suggestions of others, and read the transition’s official blog.

In a move that signals the end of traditional media monopolies on presidential communications, Obama recently released his weekly address directly to YouTube—a practice his team says will continue once he is in the White House, effectively upgrading the traditional Saturday morning radio address into an interactive, shareable video stream.

"The goal is to create a two-way conversation," said a senior transition official who spoke on the condition of anonymity. "For decades, the White House spoke *at* the American people. We want to build an architecture where the public can speak back."

### A 13-Million-Person Army

At the heart of "Obama 2.0" is the campaign’s crown jewel: an email list estimated to contain more than 13 million addresses, alongside millions of active users on platforms like Facebook and MySpace. 

Pioneered in part by Facebook co-founder Chris Hughes, who left the social network to join Obama’s campaign in 2007, the digital strategy turned passive supporters into active organizers. The administration hopes to mobilize this digital army to exert public pressure on Capitol Hill when key legislative battles—such as the proposed massive economic stimulus package—heat up later this year.

By posting draft policy proposals online and encouraging feedback, the incoming administration hopes to build public buy-in before legislation even reaches a committee vote.

However, political strategists warn that transitioning from campaigning to governing online presents unprecedented risks.

"Campaigning online is about rallying the converted," said David Gergen, a CNN senior political analyst and advisor to four presidents. "Governing is about compromise. When you open up the floor to the internet, you aren't just opening it to your supporters—you are opening it to special interests, internet trolls, and activists who may be furious when you don't follow their crowdsourced advice."

Already, the limits of online crowdsourcing have been tested. On Change.gov’s "Open for Questions" feature, the top-voted question from the public was not about the financial crisis or the war in Iraq, but about the legalization of marijuana—a policy Obama does not support.

### Cyber-Securing the Oval Office

As the transition team prepares to move into the West Wing, they are also running headfirst into the strict regulations and outdated technology of the federal government. 

The White House IT infrastructure is notoriously locked down, restricted by rigid cybersecurity protocols and the Presidential Records Act of 1978, which requires every official communication—including emails and potentially tweets or social media comments—to be archived for history.

Then there is the matter of the President-elect’s favorite gadget: his BlackBerry. 

Obama has famously expressed a desire to keep his handheld device to stay in touch with friends and staffers, defying the long-held advice of the Secret Service and White House lawyers who fear hacking and public record subpoenas. 

"I'm negotiating," Obama told CNBC in a recent interview when asked if he would have to surrender his device. "They're going to have to pry it out of my hands."

### A New Bully Pulpit

Despite the legal and technical hurdles, the transition team remains determined to drag the presidency into the digital age. Plans are reportedly underway to revamp WhiteHouse.gov the moment Obama takes the oath, transforming it into a hub for live video feeds, policy blogs, and direct public engagement.

For the Washington press corps, the rise of Obama 2.0 poses a strategic challenge. With the ability to broadcast directly to millions of Facebook feeds and YouTube channels, the White House may no longer need to rely on mainstream news networks to set the national narrative.

Yet, for a nation recovering from a deep economic downturn and weary of political polarization, the prospect of a more transparent, digitally connected government is a compelling promise.

Whether "Obama 2.0" becomes a revolutionary model for democratic engagement or simply a sophisticated tool for presidential PR remains to be seen. But one thing is clear: when Barack Obama walks into the Oval Office next week, the internet is going with him.

# Special Report: Disintermediating the Press

**Subject:** The 2008 Obama-Biden Transition Team’s Use of Digital Media to Bypass Traditional Media Filters  
**Date:** October 24, 2023  
**Prepared For:** Strategic Communications & Political History Analysis  

---

### 1. Executive Summary

Following the November 2008 presidential election, the Obama-Biden transition team (officially the Obama-Biden Transition Project) executed a paradigm shift in political communication. Building on the digital infrastructure developed during the 2008 presidential campaign, the transition team utilized custom digital platforms, social media, and direct-to-consumer video to communicate directly with the American public. 

By launching **Change.gov**, converting traditional weekly radio addresses into YouTube broadcasts, and utilizing a 13-million-person email list, the transition team successfully bypassed traditional press filters. This strategy—known in communications theory as **disintermediation**—allowed the incoming administration to set the news agenda, control messaging, crowdsource policy input, and establish a direct feedback loop with citizens, establishing a new operational blueprint for 21st-century presidential governance.

---

### 2. Historical Context & Strategic Rationale

Historically, presidential transition periods (the 75 days between Election Day and Inauguration Day) were dominated by traditional media gatekeepers: major television networks, national print newspapers, and the White House Press Corps. Information was filtered through press conferences, official statements, and selective leaks.

In 2008, the media ecosystem was undergoing a rapid digital evolution:
* **YouTube** was maturing into a dominant political platform.
* **Social Networks** (Facebook, Twitter) were shifting from social tools to news vectors.
* **Web 2.0** principles (user-generated content, interactivity) were reshaping audience expectations.

The Obama transition team recognized that relying solely on traditional media posed several risks: news cycle distortion, loss of message control, and the potential dilution of the campaign's reformist brand. To mitigate these risks, the team applied campaign-style digital mobilization strategies to official transition communications.

---

### 3. Core Digital Mechanisms Used During the Transition

#### A. Change.gov: The Digital Hub
Within days of the election, the transition team launched **Change.gov**, a dedicated website that served as the official clearinghouse for transition news. Key innovations included:
* **Direct Document Publication:** Key policy proposals, agency review team announcements, and legal applications were posted directly to the site before or simultaneously with releases to the press.
* **Creative Commons Licensing:** All content on Change.gov was published under a Creative Commons license, allowing citizens, bloggers, and local news outlets to redistribute official materials without traditional copyright or syndicate barriers.

#### B. The YouTube Address Strategy
Since the 1930s (FDR's "Fireside Chats") and formalized under President Reagan, presidents used the Saturday morning radio address to speak to the nation. The Obama transition team fundamentally restructured this medium:
* **Visual Disintermediation:** The transition team recorded high-definition video of Barack Obama delivering the weekly address and uploaded it directly to YouTube every Saturday morning.
* **Forcing TV News Integration:** Major cable networks (CNN, MSNBC, Fox News) were forced to broadcast YouTube rips or embed the official video, effectively turning mainstream media outlets into distribution channels for unedited, raw transition messaging.

#### C. Interactive Governance and Crowdsourcing
The transition team weaponized "open government" concepts to engage the public directly:
* **"Open for Questions":** A feature on Change.gov that allowed citizens to submit questions regarding policy and vote on questions submitted by others. Obama subsequently answered the top-voted questions on video.
* **The Citizen’s Briefing Book:** A digital platform where the public could submit policy ideas. Over 44,000 proposals were submitted, generating over 1.4 million votes from users.

#### D. Database & Email Mobilization
The transition team inherited the campaign’s crown jewel: a digital database containing over **13 million email addresses** and millions of cell phone numbers. 
* Rather than going dormant, this network received direct updates regarding Cabinet appointments (such as the nomination of Hillary Clinton as Secretary of State) via SMS and email *before* official announcements were made to the press corps.

---

### 4. Impact: How the Filter Was Bypassed

The transition team’s digital strategy disrupted traditional political reporting in four distinct ways:

```
[Transition Team / Change.gov] ───┬───> Direct to Public (Email, Social, YouTube)
                                   │
                                   └───> Press Gatekeepers (Forced to cover original video/raw data)
```

1. **Agenda Setting Shift:** By releasing news late at night or early morning directly on Change.gov, the transition team forced mainstream outlets to react to *their* framing, rather than journalists setting the framing through aggressive questioning.
2. **Neutralizing the "Pundit Class":** Unedited, long-form video allowed Obama to articulate complex economic strategies (in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis) without soundbites being parsed or reinterpreted by cable news pundits.
3. **Depriving the Press of "Scoops":** By publishing appointment lists and ethics guidelines directly online, the transition team flattened the information hierarchy. A small-town blogger had access to the exact same primary materials at the exact same time as a *New York Times* reporter.
4. **Maintaining a Permanent Campaign:** By keeping the 13-million-person digital network warm, the transition team created a public pressure engine that could be deployed to lobbied Congress directly regarding the incoming Recovery Act (stimulus bill).

---

### 5. Friction and Friction Points with Traditional Media

The aggressive use of direct digital communication created significant tension with the traditional press corps:

* **Complaints of Controlled Access:** Journalists argued that pre-recorded YouTube videos and curated web questions were a substitute for unscripted, tough press conferences.
* **Public Relations disguised as "Transparency":** Critics noted that while crowdsourcing platforms like "Open for Questions" offered the *illusion* of direct democracy, the transition team still retained ultimate control over which questions were addressed and how policy was finalized.
* **Archival and Legal Precedents:** The shift to third-party digital platforms raised immediate questions regarding the Presidential Records Act and data retention, forcing legal teams to rapidly build compliance protocols for social media data.

---

### 6. Legacy and Conclusion

The 2008 Obama-Biden transition team fundamentally changed the relationship between the Executive Branch, the press, and the public. By treating digital platforms not merely as broadcast tools, but as an **alternative infrastructure** to traditional media, they demonstrated that an incoming administration no longer required the press to speak to the nation.

This strategy laid the groundwork for modern digital governance. The techniques pioneered on Change.gov in late 2008 set the precedent for subsequent administrations—ranging from Donald Trump's direct use of Twitter to bypass media filters to the current White House's hyper-targeted deployment of short-form digital content creator briefings. 

Ultimately, the 2008 transition proved that in a networked digital ecosystem, direct citizen engagement can effectively marginalize traditional media gatekeepers.

"FDR had radio, JFK had television, and Barack Obama has the internet," said CNN Senior Political Analyst Bill Schneider. "What we are seeing is a fundamental shift in how a president builds and maintains political capital. It’s no longer just a top-down monologue from Washington; it’s a two-way street that bypasses the traditional media filter entirely."

The numbers behind Obama’s digital empire are staggering for a political figure. During the 2008 campaign, his team built an email list of over 13 million supporters. On Facebook, Obama boasts over 3.7 million "friends"—outpacing his political rivals by orders of magnitude—while his Twitter account reaches well over 120,000 followers, a burgeoning platform that political operatives are only beginning to understand.

Even as he prepares to move into 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue, Obama is fighting to break presidential tradition by keeping his beloved BlackBerry smartphone, raising legal and security debates inside the Secret Service and the National Security Agency.

Tech pioneers say the Obama operation marks the end of old-school political gatekeeping.

"Obama didn't just use technology to win an election; he is using it to redefine governance," said Andrew Rasiej, founder of Personal Democracy Forum, a tech and politics news site. It's not just a communications strategy—it’s crowdsourcing the presidency."

David All, a prominent Republican digital strategist and founder of the David All Group, believes Obama’s technological dominance is a wake-up call for conservative strategists.

**THE WASHINGTON DISPATCH**

**THE DIGITAL TRANSITION: How President-Elect Obama is Rewriting the Inaugural Playbook via the Web**

**By Sarah Jenkins | Technology & Politics Desk**
**WASHINGTON — January 18, 2009**

As Barack Obama prepares to take the oath of office as the 44th President of the United States this Tuesday, his team is proving that the high-tech engine that propelled his historic campaign did not shut down on Election Night. 

In the 75 days between his November victory and Inauguration Day, President-elect Obama has leveraged digital technology, social networking, and Web 2.0 tools to create the most interactive and transparent presidential transition in American history. Rather than retreating behind closed doors to assemble a cabinet, the incoming administration has used the web to maintain a direct line of communication with millions of voters, effectively turning campaign supporters into active participants in the incoming government.

### The Hub: Change.gov

At the center of this strategy is **Change.gov**, the official website of the Obama-Biden Transition Project launched just days after the election. Far from a static repository for press releases, the site was built to embody Obama’s campaign promise of "Open Government."

One of the site’s most popular interactive features, the **"Citizen’s Briefing Book,"** allowed ordinary Americans to submit policy ideas and vote up or down on proposals submitted by others. Millions of votes were cast on topics ranging from renewable energy investments to marijuana legalization. The transition team promised that the top-rated ideas would be printed and delivered directly to President Obama after he takes office.

Additionally, through the **"Open Government Initiative,"** the transition team posted thousands of public comments and policy documents online, even inviting citizens to review and critique the incoming administration's official healthcare discussions.

"We are seeing the democratization of the presidential transition," said Micah Sifry, co-founder of the Personal Democracy Forum. "Obama isn't just using the web to broadcast messages; he's using it to crowdsource public opinion and build a continuous feedback loop between the public and the White House."

### Reimagining the Weekly Address for the YouTube Era

In another break from decades of presidential tradition, Obama modernized the iconic weekly radio address pioneered by Franklin D. Roosevelt. Beginning in mid-November, Obama began releasing his weekly updates as high-definition videos posted directly to **YouTube**, in addition to traditional radio broadcasts. 

These weekly videos—addressing the looming economic crisis, national security, and cabinet appointments—frequently garnered hundreds of thousands of views within hours of posting. By bypassing traditional media gatekeepers, Obama maintained the intimate, direct connection with voters that defined his campaign, delivering his transition message directly to computer screens and mobile phones across the nation.

### Social Networks and the SMS Machine

While Change.gov served as the policy engine, established social networking sites like **Facebook, MySpace, and Twitter** served as the megaphones. The transition team actively maintained Obama's campaign profiles, which boasted millions of followers—an unprecedented reach for an incoming world leader.

In the weeks leading up to the inauguration, these platforms were used to crowdsource local civic engagement. The transition team launched a campaign urging supporters to participate in a "National Day of Service" on Martin Luther King Jr. Day, the day before the inauguration. Using interactive maps and social network integration, supporters were able to find, create, and sign up for service projects in their local communities.

Furthermore, the Obama team retained its massive, proprietary **SMS text-messaging database**—the same network used to announce Joe Biden as the vice-presidential nominee in August. In the days leading up to January 20, millions of subscribers received text messages encouraging them to submit questions for the incoming administration, sign up for local events, or stream transition press conferences live on their mobile devices.

### A New Standard for Governing

The unprecedented use of interactive digital tools during the transition period signals a fundamental shift in how the executive branch plans to operate. Obama has already pledged to create the federal government's first Chief Technology Officer (CTO) and has indicated that the digital transparency of Change.gov will transition into a revamped WhiteHouse.gov immediately following the swearing-in ceremony.

As Washington fills with an estimated two million visitors arriving for Tuesday’s ceremonies, millions more will be participating virtually. By transforming passive voters into active digital participants during the transition, Barack Obama has not only set a new standard for political communication, but has also laid the foundation for the first true "Internet Presidency."

At the heart of this digital empire was *My.BarackObama.com*—or "MyBO"—a custom-built social network spearheaded by 25-year-old Facebook co-founder Chris Hughes. The platform allowed more than 2 million supporters to create local profile pages, organize over 200,000 offline events, and launch hyper-targeted door-knocking drives in crucial swing states like Ohio and Florida without ever waiting for orders from headquarters.

The results smashed every record in political history. 

Through a massive, 13-million-address email list and simple online forms, the Obama campaign disproved the long-held political myth that presidential candidates must rely solely on deep-pocketed lobbyists and corporate bundlers. The digital campaign was equally adept at direct communication. When Obama selected Delaware Sen. Joe Biden as his running mate in August, nearly 3 million supporters learned the news via a midnight text message—an unprecedented use of mobile technology that circumvented the traditional press corps and delivered news straight to the voters' pockets.
